name: Sesamoid Bones of the Hallux (grouped)
text: Mainly one sesamoid artery into each proximal pole: medial plantar (posterior tibial) or first plantar metatarsal artery, by study. Minor plantar and capsular vessels.
notes: Disagreement on the main artery: Chamberland 1993 names the medial plantar artery; Rath 2009 names the first plantar metatarsal artery. Owner call: Poor rests on single-vessel dependence plus documented AVN and nonunion, not on a named watershed.

zone.text: Whole bone: mainly one vessel into the proximal pole; avascular necrosis and nonunion are documented.

zone.text: The cartilage matrix itself: avascular, fed by diffusion from the perichondrium.

StatPearls: Proximal Humerus Fracture

quotes.title: Predictors of humeral head ischemia after intracapsular fracture of the proximal humerus
quotes.quote: When the above criteria (anatomic neck, short calcar, disrupted hinge) were combined, positive predictive values of up to 97% could be obtained.
quotes.citation: Hertel R, Hempfing A, Stiehler M, Leunig M. J Shoulder Elbow Surg. 2004;13(4):427-33. PMID 15220884

quotes.title: Quantitative assessment of the vascularity of the proximal part of the humerus
quotes.quote: The posterior humeral circumflex artery provided 64% of the blood supply to the humeral head overall, whereas the anterior humeral circumflex artery supplied 36%.
quotes.citation: Hettrich CM, Boraiah S, Dyke JP, Neviaser A, Helfet DL, Lorich DG. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2010;92(4):943-8. PMID 20360519

quotes.title: StatPearls: Proximal Humerus Fracture
quotes.quote: The posterior humeral circumflex artery is the main blood supply to the humeral head.

ratingWhy: Poor: AVN-prone region: an anatomic-neck fracture line is one of the criteria that, combined with a short calcar and a disrupted medial hinge, predicts humeral head ischaemia with up to 97% positive predictive value.

name: Medial Epicondyle of Humerus
text: Medial arcade of the elbow anastomosis: superior and inferior ulnar collateral, anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries
notes: Yamaguchi et al. found watershed areas between the medial and lateral supply of the distal humerus. That applies to the articular trochlea and capitellum, not the epicondyle. Neither source measures supply inside the epicondyle.

sources.title: Gray's Anatomy (1918): The Brachial Artery
The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow

quotes.title: Gray's Anatomy (1918): The Brachial Artery
quotes.quote: The branches anastomosing in front of the medial epicondyle are: the anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral, the anterior ulnar recurrent, and the anterior branch of the superior ulnar collateral. Those behind the medial epicondyle are: the inferior ulnar collateral, the posterior ulnar recurrent, and the posterior branch of the superior ulnar collateral.

quotes.title: The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
quotes.quote: The medial arcade was formed by the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries and the posterior ulnar recurrent artery.
quotes.citation: Yamaguchi K, Sweet FA, Bindra R, Morrey BF, Gelberman RH. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1997;79(11):1653-62. PMID 9384425

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy: several named arteries anastomose in front of and behind the epicondyle, over extra-articular cancellous bone.

name: Lateral Epicondyle of Humerus
text: Lateral arcade of the elbow anastomosis: radial recurrent, radial and middle collateral, and interosseous recurrent arteries
notes: The documented watershed is between the medial and lateral halves of the articular distal humerus, not in the epicondyle itself. Gray's also lists the inferior ulnar collateral behind the lateral epicondyle.

sources.title: Gray's Anatomy (1918): The Brachial Artery
The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow

quotes.title: Gray's Anatomy (1918): The Brachial Artery
quotes.quote: The branches anastomosing in front of the lateral epicondyle are: the radial recurrent and the terminal part of the profunda brachii. Those behind the lateral epicondyle (perhaps more properly described as being situated between the lateral epicondyle and the olecranon) are: the inferior ulnar collateral, the interosseous recurrent, and the radial collateral branch of the profunda brachii.

quotes.title: The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
quotes.quote: The lateral arcade was formed by the radial and middle collateral, radial recurrent, and interosseous recurrent arteries.
quotes.citation: Yamaguchi K, Sweet FA, Bindra R, Morrey BF, Gelberman RH. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1997;79(11):1653-62. PMID 9384425

quotes.title: The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
quotes.quote: Watershed areas were apparent between the blood supplies to the medial and lateral aspects of the distal end of the humerus.
quotes.citation: Yamaguchi K, Sweet FA, Bindra R, Morrey BF, Gelberman RH. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1997;79(11):1653-62. PMID 9384425

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy: several named arteries anastomose in front of and behind the epicondyle, over extra-articular cancellous bone.

name: Coronoid Process of Ulna
text: Proximal ulnar arterial network: anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries medially, interosseous recurrent laterally
notes: No source names the coronoid itself. Koslowsky et al. found an intraosseous 'transitional zone' in the proximal ulna but the abstract does not say where; a full-text check could matter for the coronoid or trochlear notch. Koslowsky's 'anterior artery' is read as the anterior ulnar recurrent artery.

sources.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Ulna
Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique

quotes.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: Proximal ulna vascularization is due to an arterial network [...]. An anterior artery and a posterior recurrent artery climb up distally to the medial parts of the ulna and an interosseous recurrent artery is responsible for the lateral and posterolateral proximal part of the ulna.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Berger V, Hopf JC, Muller LP. Surg Radiol Anat. 2015;37(7):749-55. PMID 25894529

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Ulna
quotes.quote: The main blood supply of the ulna originates from the ulnar artery or the ulnar recurrent artery.

quotes.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: A transitional zone of the intraosseous vascularization of the proximal ulna was detected.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Berger V, Hopf JC, Muller LP. Surg Radiol Anat. 2015;37(7):749-55. PMID 25894529

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy (regional): the proximal ulna is fed by a documented multi-vessel network, and it is cancellous bone.

name: Trochlear Notch
text: Bone behind the notch is fed by the proximal ulnar network (ulnar recurrent and interosseous recurrent arteries); the articular lining is avascular
notes: Articular (hyaline) cartilage on this surface is avascular and fed by diffusion; the rating is for the bone beneath. Koslowsky et al. report an unlocated intraosseous transitional zone in the proximal ulna. Call for the owner: rate the notch as bone (Rich), or as an articular surface.

sources.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique

quotes.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: Proximal ulna vascularization is due to an arterial network [...]. An anterior artery and a posterior recurrent artery climb up distally to the medial parts of the ulna and an interosseous recurrent artery is responsible for the lateral and posterolateral proximal part of the ulna.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Berger V, Hopf JC, Muller LP. Surg Radiol Anat. 2015;37(7):749-55. PMID 25894529

quotes.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: The intraosseous vascularization is due to directly penetrating branches out of the posterior recurrent ulnar artery and a vascular plexus at the olecranon tip.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Berger V, Hopf JC, Muller LP. Surg Radiol Anat. 2015;37(7):749-55. PMID 25894529

quotes.title: Presentation of the vascular supply of the proximal ulna using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: A transitional zone of the intraosseous vascularization of the proximal ulna was detected.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Berger V, Hopf JC, Muller LP. Surg Radiol Anat. 2015;37(7):749-55. PMID 25894529

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy (regional): proximal-ulna network over cancellous bone. The cartilage surface of the notch is avascular (tissue baseline).

name: Head of Radius
text: Radial recurrent artery directly, plus vessels entering at the neck through the capsule (pericervical ring from the radial recurrent and an ulnar periosteal branch)
notes: Articular (hyaline) cartilage on this surface is avascular and fed by diffusion; the rating is for the bone beneath. The two studies differ on the medial source. Yamaguchi et al. give radial and interosseous recurrent vessels; Koslowsky et al. give a periosteal branch of the ulnar artery, with the interosseous recurrent at the neck.

sources.title: The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
Presentation of the microscopic vascular architecture of the radial head using a sequential plastination technique
Presentation of the microscopic vascular architecture of the radial head using a sequential plastination technique

quotes.title: The extraosseous and intraosseous arterial anatomy of the adult elbow
quotes.quote: The radial head had a dual extraosseous blood supply from a single branch of the radial recurrent artery, which supplied the head directly, and from additional vessels from both the radial and the interosseous recurrent artery, which penetrated the capsular insertion at the neck of the radius.
quotes.citation: Yamaguchi K, Sweet FA, Bindra R, Morrey BF, Gelberman RH. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1997;79(11):1653-62. PMID 9384425

quotes.title: Presentation of the microscopic vascular architecture of the radial head using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: Vascularization of the radial head occurred via branches of the radial recurrent artery on the ventral, lateral, and dorsal sides of the radial head and a branch of the ulnar artery--ramus periostalis ulnaris--medially and dorsomedially. Both arteries create a pericervical arterial ring around the radial neck.
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Schliwa S, Koebke J. Clin Anat. 2011;24(6):721-32. PMID 21671281

quotes.title: Presentation of the microscopic vascular architecture of the radial head using a sequential plastination technique
quotes.quote: Besides devascularization of the radial head due to the injury leading to a certain risk of fracture nonunion
quotes.citation: Koslowsky TC, Schliwa S, Koebke J. Clin Anat. 2011;24(6):721-32. PMID 21671281

ratingWhy: Moderate: Supply anatomy and location: a dual supply, but the head is intra-articular and cartilage-covered. Vessels reach it through the capsule at the neck, and injury can devascularise it.

name: Radial Tuberosity
text: Radial and radial recurrent arteries (proximal radius), the radial recurrent anastomosing with the radial collateral artery
notes: No source addresses the tuberosity itself.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Radius
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Radius
quotes.quote: The blood supply to the proximal radius is provided primarily by the radial and radial recurrent arteries. The radial recurrent artery travels proximally to anastomose with the radial collateral artery.

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones
quotes.quote: Additionally, smaller branches supplying the proximal radius originated from the radial artery, while the distal radius also received penetrating vessels from the palmar arterial arches.

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy (regional): the proximal radius has more than one source with an anastomosis, and it is extra-articular bone.

name: Ulnar Styloid Process
text: Distal ulna: small branches of the ulnar artery and the radial–ulnar–anterior interosseous anastomoses
notes: Call for the owner: the high nonunion rate is usually put down to TFCC traction and the fracture being left untreated, not to proven poor perfusion; no source makes a vascular claim for the styloid. Held at Moderate rather than Poor for that reason.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Ulna
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones
StatPearls: Distal Ulnar Fractures

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Ulna
quotes.quote: The ulnar metaphysis is supplied by the end branches of the anterior interosseous artery, while the head of the ulna receives its supply from small divisions off of the ulnar artery proper.

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones
quotes.quote: The ulna receives small vessel input from the ulnar recurrent artery proximally, and similar to the distal radius, the distal ulna receives input from branches of the anastomoses between the radial artery, the ulnar artery, and the anterior interosseous artery.

quotes.title: StatPearls: Distal Ulnar Fractures
quotes.quote: Ulnar styloid nonunion is frequently encountered, with an incidence between 20% to 70%.

ratingWhy: Moderate: Supply anatomy: small vessels from an anastomotic network. The clinical proxy is mixed, because styloid fractures often fail to unite (20–70%).

name: Radial Styloid Process
text: Distal radius: radial, anterior and posterior interosseous arteries, plus penetrating vessels from the palmar arches
notes: No source addresses the radial styloid specifically.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Radius
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Radius
quotes.quote: Blood supply to the middle and distal radius is through the radial, posterior interosseous, and anterior interosseous arteries.

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Forearm Bones
quotes.quote: Additionally, smaller branches supplying the proximal radius originated from the radial artery, while the distal radius also received penetrating vessels from the palmar arterial arches.

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy (regional): the distal radius has several sources, including arch vessels, over cancellous metaphyseal bone.

name: Scaphoid
arteries: Superficial palmar branch of the radial artery
text: Radial artery: dorsal carpal branches enter the dorsal ridge and run backwards to the proximal pole; palmar branches supply the distal pole
notes: StatPearls (Carpal Bones) calls it a single supply from the radial artery. The Scaphoid Fracture chapter names the dorsal carpal branch plus a distal palmar source from the superficial palmar arch. Both describe the radial artery and the same retrograde pattern.

zone.text: Proximal pole: supplied retrogradely, so fractures of the waist or proximal third can leave it without blood (AVN up to 100% in proximal fractures).

sources.title: StatPearls: Scaphoid Wrist Fracture
StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
The vascularity of the wrist. Identification of arterial patterns at risk
StatPearls: Scaphoid Wrist Fracture

quotes.title: StatPearls: Scaphoid Wrist Fracture
quotes.quote: Blood supply to the scaphoid bone is predominantly from branches of the radial artery (dorsal carpal branch). These enter the dorsal ridge and supply 80% of the proximal pole via retrograde flow. The second source is from the superficial palmar arch, a branch of the volar radial artery, which enters the distal tubercle and supplies the distal pole.

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
quotes.quote: The scaphoid, capitate, and a small proportion of lunates (20%) have 1 intraosseous vessel supply. Of note, the scaphoid has a single blood supply from the radial artery that enters from the distal portion of the bone to supply the proximal portion, thus making its proximal pole most vulnerable to avascular necrosis.

quotes.title: The vascularity of the wrist. Identification of arterial patterns at risk
quotes.quote: Group 1, which consisted of the scaphoid, the capitate, and eight percent of the lunates, had either vessels entering only one surface or large areas of bone that were dependent on a single vessel. This group was the most vulnerable to posttraumatic avascular necrosis.
quotes.citation: Gelberman RH, Gross MS. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1986;(202):40-9. PMID 3514029

quotes.title: StatPearls: Scaphoid Wrist Fracture
quotes.quote: The incidence of avascular necrosis carries a strong association with the location of the fracture; the proximal segment has a 100% rate of AVN, reducing to 33% at the distal segment of the scaphoid.

ratingWhy: Poor: Retrograde flow: about 80% of the proximal pole is fed backwards from vessels entering distally, so waist fractures can cut off the proximal pole (avascular necrosis, nonunion).

name: Lunate
text: Variable dorsal and palmar penetrating vessels from the radiocarpal and intercarpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries); intraosseous collaterals sparse
notes: Disagreement worth knowing: Gelberman & Gross put 92% of lunates in the richly anastomosed, lowest-risk group. Poor follows the brief, which lists the lunate among AVN-prone bones; most individual lunates are well supplied. StatPearls gives 20% single-vessel lunates; Gelberman gives 8%.

zone.text: Lunates with a single (volar or dorsal) supply or no intraosseous anastomosis (7–26% lack one side; up to 7.5% have no anastomosis; about 8–20% single-vessel) are the ones at risk of Kienböck disease.

sources.title: StatPearls: Kienbock Disease

StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones

quotes.title: StatPearls: Kienbock Disease
quotes.quote: The lunate receives blood from a variable number of dorsal and volar penetrating arteries that arise from the dorsal and palmar radiocarpal and intercarpal arches. Intraosseous collateral vessels are sparse.

quotes.title: Vascularity of the lunate. Anatomic studies and implications for the development of osteonecrosis
quotes.quote: The dorsal and volar arterial systems anastomose distal to the midline of the lunate; however, in as many as 7.5% of lunates, no anastomosis my be present. Between 7% and 26% of lunates may lack either a volar or dorsal arterial supply.
quotes.citation: Williams CS, Gelberman RH. Hand Clin. 1993;9(3):391-8. PMID 8408249

quotes.title: The vascularity of the wrist. Identification of arterial patterns at risk
quotes.quote: Group 3 bones, which included the trapezium, the triquetrum, the pisiform, and 92% of the lunates, had rich internal anastomoses and were at least risk of undergoing avascular necrosis.
quotes.citation: Gelberman RH, Gross MS. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1986;(202):40-9. PMID 3514029

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
quotes.quote: The scaphoid, capitate, and a small proportion of lunates (20%) have 1 intraosseous vessel supply. Of note, the scaphoid has a single blood supply from the radial artery that enters from the distal portion of the bone to supply the proximal portion, thus making its proximal pole most vulnerable to avascular necrosis.

ratingWhy: Poor: AVN-prone bone: the lunate is the second most common carpal bone to undergo avascular necrosis (Kienböck disease). A minority of lunates have a single vessel or no internal anastomosis.

name: Triquetrum
text: Dorsal and palmar carpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries); two areas of supply with consistent intraosseous anastomoses
notes: StatPearls likely draws on the Gelberman studies, so the two sources are not fully independent.

sources.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
quotes.quote: The trapezoid and hamate both have 2 blood supply areas without intraosseous anastomoses. The trapezium, triquetrum, pisiform, and most lunates (80%) have 2 areas of blood supply and consistent intraosseous anastomoses.

quotes.title: The vascularity of the wrist. Identification of arterial patterns at risk
quotes.quote: Group 3 bones, which included the trapezium, the triquetrum, the pisiform, and 92% of the lunates, had rich internal anastomoses and were at least risk of undergoing avascular necrosis.
quotes.citation: Gelberman RH, Gross MS. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1986;(202):40-9. PMID 3514029

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
quotes.quote: In particular, vascular supply occurs via the anastomotic network consisting of 3 dorsal and 3 palmar arches, which arise from both the radial and ulnar arteries that overlie the carpal bones.

ratingWhy: Rich: Supply anatomy: two entry areas with rich internal anastomoses, in the lowest-risk group for avascular necrosis.

name: Pisiform
text: Dorsal and palmar carpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries); two areas of supply with consistent intraosseous anastomoses
notes: StatPearls likely draws on the Gelberman studies, so the two sources are not fully independent. No source here names the specific branch to the pisiform.

text: Dorsal and palmar carpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries); two areas of supply but no intraosseous anastomosis
notes: StatPearls likely draws on the Gelberman studies, so the two sources are not fully independent.

quotes.quote: The trapezoid and hamate both have 2 blood supply areas without intraosseous anastomoses. The trapezium, triquetrum, pisiform, and most lunates (80%) have 2 areas of blood supply and consistent intraosseous anastomoses.

quotes.title: The vascularity of the wrist. Identification of arterial patterns at risk
quotes.quote: The bones of Group 2, the hamate and the trapezoid, were characterized by the absence of internal anastomoses. Although these bones are theoretically at risk, they do not undergo avascular necrosis.
quotes.citation: Gelberman RH, Gross MS. Clin Orthop Relat Res. 1986;(202):40-9. PMID 3514029

quotes.title: StatPearls: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones
quotes.quote: In particular, vascular supply occurs via the anastomotic network consisting of 3 dorsal and 3 palmar arches, which arise from both the radial and ulnar arteries that overlie the carpal bones.

ratingWhy: Moderate: Supply anatomy: two entry areas without internal anastomoses. It is theoretically at risk, but avascular necrosis does not occur in practice.

name: Capitate
text: Dorsal and palmar carpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries), but a single intraosseous vessel system feeds large areas of the bone
notes: Neither source here names the proximal pole (head) of the capitate as the at-risk part, so the zone is left general. Capitate AVN is clinically uncommon compared with the scaphoid.

zone.text: Large areas of the bone depend on a single vessel entering one surface.

ratingWhy: Poor: End-artery pattern: large areas depend on a single vessel, so a purely intraosseous disruption (a fracture) can cause avascular necrosis.

name: Hamate
text: Dorsal and palmar carpal arches (radial and ulnar arteries); trunk vessels enter dorsal and volar non-articular surfaces
notes: Sources disagree on anastomosis. Gelberman & Gross say it is absent. Xiao et al. found dorsal–volar arterial arches in 5 of 6 hamates. The hook is rated separately (Poor).

quotes.title: Features of intra-hamate vascularity and its possible relationship with avascular risk of hamate fracture
quotes.quote: The abundant blood supply obviously contributes to the high healing rate of fracture of the hamate body.
quotes.citation: Xiao ZR, Zhang WG, Xiong G. Chin Med J (Engl). 2019;132(21):2572-2580. PMID 31658154

ratingWhy: Moderate: Supply anatomy: two entry areas. Older injection work found no internal anastomosis, but a micro-CT study describes abundant supply and high union rates in the body.

name: Hook of Hamate
text: Small vessels entering mainly from the palmar (volar) surface of the hamate body and at the hook tip; the middle of the hook is least supplied
notes: arteries left empty: no source here names the parent artery of the hook's vessels. Xiao et al. say older foramen-counting studies (Failla) overstate the tip supply. The 50% nonunion figure is for non-displaced hook fractures treated in a cast.

zone.text: Middle part of the hook, between a better-supplied base and tip.

name: Glenohumeral Joint
text: Capsule supplied by the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, with the suprascapular artery.
notes: The articular (hyaline) cartilage itself is avascular and nourished by diffusion from synovial fluid; the rating is for the capsule and synovium. Gray's 'transverse scapular' is the old name for the suprascapular artery. The StatPearls section also says 'The subscapular artery, arising from the thyrocervical trunk' - the subscapular artery arises from the axillary artery, so this looks like a slip for suprascapular; not used. The 64%/34% PCHA/ACHA split in StatPearls refers to the humeral head (bone), not the capsule.

zone.text: Glenoid labrum: vascular only at its periphery, and the superior and anterosuperior labrum is less vascular than the posterosuperior and inferior parts.

quotes.title: Gray's Anatomy of the Human Body (1918)
quotes.quote: The arteries supplying the joint are articular branches of the anterior and posterior humeral circumflex, and transverse scapular.

quotes.title: Anatomy, histology, and vascularity of the glenoid labrum
quotes.quote: The arteries supplying the periphery of the glenoid labrum come from the suprascapular, circumflex scapular, and posterior circumflex humeral arteries. In general, the superior and anterosuperior parts of the labrum have less vascularity than do the posterosuperior and inferior parts, and the vascularity is limited to the periphery of the labrum.
quotes.citation: Cooper DE, Arnoczky SP, O'Brien SJ, Warren RF, DiCarlo E, Allen AA. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1992;74(1):46-52.

ratingWhy: Moderate: Supply anatomy: two circumflex humeral arteries plus the suprascapular, which anastomose; but capsule and synovium are intermediate-vascularity tissue, so Moderate under the framework.
